name: Psychodermatology

card.summary: A mind-body approach to skin care that treats stress, anxiety and psychological factors alongside conditions such as acne, eczema and psoriasis, to help skin look clearer and calmer.
card.note: Terms like psychodermatology and neurocosmetics are also used in cosmetic marketing; psychiatric medicines used in the field are prescription-only.

quick.overview:
Psychodermatology studies and treats the two-way link between the mind and the skin. Stress can aggravate acne, eczema, psoriasis, rosacea, hair loss and itch, and visible skin disease in turn affects mood and confidence, so treating both sides is meant to improve how skin looks and how people feel about it.

A clinical review estimates psychiatric comorbidity in up to one third of dermatology patients. Care ranges from stress management, psychotherapy and psychoeducation to psychiatric medication for conditions such as skin picking, hair pulling or body dysmorphic disorder, plus a growing cosmetic interest in the skin-brain axis.
quick.how: In practice it means a dermatologist, sometimes together with a psychologist or psychiatrist, treats the skin condition and the stress, habits or mood symptoms around it. Approaches described in reviews include psychotherapy, relaxation, behavioural habit-reversal, psychoeducation and, where indicated, psychotropic medicines. Skin-care users encounter the term mostly through stress-and-skin advice.
quick.risks: The medications used in the field, such as antidepressants and antipsychotics, have their own safety profiles and are prescribed by clinicians. Reviews also note that psychodermatology patients may not recognise a psychological contribution, which makes some cases hard to treat. The label is unregulated in cosmetics marketing.

lead: Psychodermatology is the field that sits between dermatology and psychiatry, studying psychocutaneous conditions that have both skin and psychological aspects [1]. Its appearance payoff is straightforward: when stress makes acne, eczema, psoriasis or rosacea flare, or when skin picking or hair pulling damages the skin, addressing the psychological driver can help the skin look better [2].

Reviews divide the conditions into three groups. Psychophysiologic disorders are skin diseases worsened by emotional stress, such as urticaria, eczema, psoriasis, acne, seborrheic dermatitis, alopecia areata and rosacea. Primary psychiatric disorders produce skin changes and include trichotillomania, neurotic excoriations, factitial dermatitis, delusions of parasitosis and body dysmorphic disorder. Secondary psychiatric disorders arise from living with a visible skin condition [2][3].

Mechanistically, the field draws on the interplay between nervous, endocrine and immune systems; stress hormones such as cortisol can disrupt the skin barrier and inflame conditions like atopic dermatitis [4][5]. A recent strand of the literature extends this to a skin-brain axis and 'neurocosmetics' [6]. Wikipedia notes that the field has had limited conclusive data and that critics argue medicine is already holistic, and that cosmetics marketers use the term loosely [7].

chain: Stress and psychological factors aggravate skin disease or drive picking
Treat stress, habits and mood alongside the skin
Fewer flares and less self-inflicted damage, clearer skin
angle.text: People use it to calm stress-sensitive skin and to address habits such as picking that leave marks. The skin gains come through reduced flares and less damage rather than a topical effect.

paras: Psychodermatologic disorders involve an interaction between the mind and skin. Authors estimate that effective management in at least one third of dermatology patients involves emotional factors [8]. Patients with primary psychiatric conditions frequently lack insight into a psychological cause and so are among the more challenging to treat [3].

Dermatologists commonly encounter patients needing psychopharmacology, and reviews cover antidepressants, antipsychotics and anxiolytics with their safety profiles in dermatology [9]. Non-drug approaches include psychotherapy, relaxation and hypnosis, and a pilot randomised trial tested a short psychoeducational schema-therapy intervention in patients with psoriasis or atopic dermatitis who had elevated depression screening scores [7][10].

Recent reviews describe skin as a neuroendocrine organ that communicates with the central nervous system through hormones, cytokines and neurotransmitters, and discuss UV exposure, cortisol and brain ageing [11]. A 2025 commentary introduces neurocosmetics as skincare aimed at emotional wellbeing through this axis [6].
Cosmetic brands use psychodermatology and neurocosmetics as marketing language, and these terms are not regulated [7]. Stress management for skin is also a common theme in online skincare discussion.

Randomised trials exist for specific interventions. A trial in healthcare workers with hand eczema during the COVID-19 pandemic used a psychodermatological framing while comparing an emollient cream with standard treatment [12]. A German pilot crossover trial tested psychoeducational schema therapy in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis [10]. A trial on classical conditioning and observational learning examined nocebo effects on experimentally induced itch [13]. Overall, much of the literature consists of reviews describing conditions and clinical experience [2][3].

timeline.event: A Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology update reviews the field and notes emotional factors in at least a third of dermatology patients [8].
A review in the Primary Care Companion to the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry classifies common psychocutaneous disorders and treatments [14].
Reviews frame the skin-brain axis and neurocosmetics as an emerging area [6][11].
